story.text: Once upon a time in the 1960s, a boy and a girl met at college. We’ll call them Robert and Linda.
A few years later, during an unusually rainy season in January, they started dating.
Then a few years after that, they got married.
Eventually they had two kids, bought a single-family home, and built successful careers.

Decades later, in 2017, Robert was asked how his relationship is.


He said it was excellent.

Robert is one of the thousands of adults Stanford University researchers have been [tracking](https://data.stanford.edu/hcmst2017) to understand how couples meet, how they separate, and what their relationships are like. Here, I’ve grouped everyone on the screen by their relationship status in 2017.
This piece only visualizes people who participated in all three waves of this survey.
For now, most partnered people say their relationships are excellent or good.
Men are slightly more likely to say their relationship is excellent . >> Chart Data|filler
People with more money tend to report better relationships —partially because they have more time and resources to devote to their partners.
Also, older people have had more time to find and develop high-quality relationships.

But over time, fewer and fewer people have said their relationships are excellent—and that aligns with some concerning trends.


More people report being unsatisfied with their marriage.


>> Marriage satisfaction Data|filler


And the dynamics in those relationships have shifted in worrying ways.


From 1987 to 2013, both [married couples](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36683860/) and [cohabitating partners](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11113-025-09982-y) reported more unfairness and disagreement. They also said they interacted less with their partners, [possibly](https://www.theatlantic.com/health/archive/2017/09/we-expect-way-too-much-from-our-romantic-partners/541353/) because many Americans are working longer hours to make ends meet.


>> Charts Data|filler


Given these circumstances, some researchers suspected that a societal disruption like a pandemic could expose the fractures in our relationships—eroding or even breaking them. This is called [stress theory](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7644604/), which argues that these stressors actually use up the very energy we need to support our partners through it. This is especially true of [chronic stressors](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2352250X16300690), like financial strain and long-term illness, which constantly sip away at the emotional capacity we need to care for both a relationship and our own well-being.


But if couples can successfully navigate these challenges, researchers have found that it brings couples closer together—a framework called [resilience theory](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1545-5300.2003.00001.x). They are able to build a shared meaning of the threat, come up with a plan, and rely on each other to weather the events.

It’s 2020. A global pandemic begins.


Within the confines of their locked down home, Robert and Linda have agreed that they should socially distance and wear masks in public.
They haven’t fought much during lockdown, unlike some couples.

In fact, Robert says his relationship is still excellent—just like before.


Not a huge surprise, given that they’ve been together for more than 50 years!
But what happened to everyone else we met in 2017?

story.chart_title: How relationship quality changed from 2017 to 2020
story.text:
Love stories hypnotize us with scripts of what a relationship should look like. They give us templates for courting, proposals, marriage, and even domestic life.


Those stories shape the expectations we have for relationships—but the stories have shifted drastically over time. Relationship historians like [Andrew J. Cherlin](https://www.jstor.org/stable/3600162) break down modern conceptions of American marriage into three eras. 


>> Three eras|filler


**Before the 1850s**, marriage was about survival. Partnerships were about ensuring financial success, while continuing your family line. It certainly wasn’t about a strong emotional connection with another person.


**From the 1850s to 1960s**, marriage slowly became more about companionship—but following a rigid script. People were expected to fill specific gender roles as breadwinners, homemakers, and parents. Furthermore, sex and children were only socially acceptable in a marriage, so almost everyone got married.


>> Charts on marriage rates + median age of marriage|filler


But during this era, something was brewing under the surface. Sociologist [Francesca Cancian](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/089124388002003006) analyzed the kind of marriage advice popular magazines offered in each decade, and she found that traditional expectations were replaced by advice that urged people to shape their relationship based on their own preferences.


In other words, people rebelled against the stories.

>> Cancian Data|filler


**Since the 1960s**, marriage has become less about fulfilling societal gender roles, and more about negotiating a partnership that works for us both inside and outside our relationships. We want a partner who can allow us to develop into the person we want to be—and it doesn’t even have to include marriage.


Sociologist Eli J. Finkel [argues](https://www.nytimes.com/2014/02/15/opinion/sunday/the-all-or-nothing-marriage.html) that our evolving expectations of relationships have followed Maslow’s hierarchy of needs. Initially we chose our relationships based on survival; then we wanted to feel loved; and then we wanted relationships that helped us be the people we want to be.


>> Maslow Psychological well being/safety, belonging/love, self-actualization|filler


That said, the classic love story still captures our imaginations. So that means we want relationships that provide security, passion, intellectual stimulation, and personal growth. We expect more from our partners than ever before—an “all-or-nothing” arrangement, Finkel [says](https://www.amazon.com/All-Nothing-Marriage-Best-Marriages/dp/052595516X).


When our relationships can’t meet our high and sometimes rigid expectations, we’re unsatisfied.


But when our relationships live up to these expectations—especially in the face of an external threat—we’re happier than ever.

story.text: When asked about the quality of their relationship, the top of the rating scale is excellent. But something interesting is under the surface.

First, let’s sort these people by their relationship quality.


And then let’s ask them a question: How did the pandemic change your relationship?

story.chart_title: Agreement on safety measures during the pandemic?
story.text: And couples in excellent relationships were far more likely to have complete agreement on what safety measures they should follow during the pandemic. A 63-year-old man [told](https://web.stanford.edu/~mrosenfe/Rosenfeld_Hausen_Resilience_Stress_Soc_Sci_2023.pdf) researchers, “We have given up the outside world to keep each other safe. You see, I love [wife’s name] so much.”

story.chart_title: Agreement on safety measures during the pandemic?
story.text:
The way couples responded to the pandemic gives us a big hint as to why some of these partnerships are so strong.


Stanford researchers [found](https://web.stanford.edu/~mrosenfe/Rosenfeld_Hausen_Resilience_Stress_Soc_Sci_2023.pdf) that functional couples engaged in “mutual meaning making.” They aligned their perspectives on the virus’s risk, and agreed on how they would behave in response to it. 


And when they didn’t?


“A big wedge has been driven between us on how exactly to handle the virus,” a 22-year-old woman told researchers. “I want to wear a mask, gloves, limit exposure as much as humanly possible, I wipe down surfaces and use hand sanitizer. He thinks I’m being, in his words, ‘ridiculous and paranoid.’ “


Psychologist John Gottman, who has observed thousands of couples, says that building a life with a shared sense of meaning and purpose is important. In fact, he puts that at the very top of his “Sound Relationship House”—the components that make up a strong relationship.


>> The Sound Relationship House|filler


“I believe that everyone is a philosopher trying to make some sense out of this brief journey we have through life,” Gottman writes in his book, [The Science of Trust](https://wwnorton.com/books/9780393705959). “People do that in many ways, including creating formal and informal rituals of connection, creating shared  goals and life missions, supporting each other’s basic roles in life, and agreeing on the meaning of central values and symbols (like ‘what is a home?’).”


And he writes that it all starts from building a “love map” of your partner.


”It’s about feeling like your partner is interested in knowing you, and your partner feeling that you are interested in knowing her or him,” he writes.
These days, people often focus on how there are more single people now than ever before. >> Chart Data from Pew|filler
They point out that a lot of people report having worse relationships than before.

story.text: Furthermore, single people are [less interested](https://www.rasmussenreports.com/public_content/lifestyle/general_lifestyle/june_2025/dating_37_of_young_singles_aren_t_interested) in pursuing romance than in prior generations. >> Chart Data|filler
If we first group these people by how long they’ve been in a relationship…

… we can see that online dating is how most new relationships start these days. And people [really don’t enjoy](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/archive/2024/04/dating-apps-are-starting-crack/678022/) online dating.

The world doesn’t look the way it does in our love stories. So it’s tempting to believe that we just need to go back to those scripts.


A [recent survey](https://www.kcl.ac.uk/news/almost-a-third-of-gen-z-men-agree-a-wife-should-obey-her-husband) found that Gen Z men worldwide are more likely to have traditional views on relationships than the last three generations. 


>> Charts|filler


Even though dating has moved online, about [90%](https://phys.org/news/2022-02-discrepancy-hookup-culture-sexual-dates.html) of dates among young people are still initiated by men.


And in heterosexual relationships, women still do [more household work](https://fraser.stlouisfed.org/files/docs/releases/atus/atus_20250626.pdf) than men. This doesn’t even include the [mental labor](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0003122419859007) women do to keep a household functioning.


But when we default back to these traditional love stories, we end up being characters in our own lives—and we end up treating our partners that way, too. It’s a story that expects women to be submissive and deferential to men, while being responsible for most of the domestic work. It expects men to play the role of provider and protector, even when their families need them to be nurturers and caretakers.


This story doesn’t require us to build love maps of each other. Instead it tells us all we have to do is follow the script.
But I’d prefer to live in a story that works for me and the person I love most in this world—a story that takes place on our overlapping love maps.
Because we aren’t characters in some fairy tale. We are two people who want to spend the rest of our lives together, and that’s a good enough story as it is.
